title: Only God is necessary being: real being divides into creator and creature
english: First Exercise. On being and essence.
Article I. The first division of real being is set out, and it is shown that God alone is necessary being.

Real being is first divided into finite and infinite — that is, into creator and creature. This division is commonly handed down and proposed in many other ways. Some put it thus: one being is from itself, another from another. Others thus: of beings, some are or exist by essence, others by participation. Others thus: one being is necessary, another contingent. The glorious God is infinite being, having existence from no other; he is likewise being by essence, and supremely necessary. Creatures, however, are finite beings, having existence from another; and therefore they are not necessary, but contingent.

2. The first two ways of proposing this division need no explanation; the last two are not so clear, and therefore they call for a longer account. I will begin from the last division, which is into necessary being and contingent being. The glorious God is called necessary being because it is necessary that he always exist in act. For God cannot deprive himself of his own being — that is, of the act of existence — nor can anything else do so, since he does not depend on another. Creatures, however, are contingent beings; that is, they exist contingently. For they hang upon the conserving power of a freely acting cause — that is, of God — who, before he gave them being, could have refused to give it, and after he has given it can take it away.

3. Many objections are usually raised here about the necessity of separated substances, of the heavenly bodies, of prime matter, of universal natures, and of necessary propositions, to which philosophers ascribe eternal truth. But because those thorny questions deter many by their difficulty and call them away from philosophical studies, I omit them and go on to other matters that are more necessary and more pleasant.
translator_notes: Tip only: Exercitatio Prima Art. I from the 1658 Oxford corrected reprint. Not the whole Philosophia theologiae ancillans.

No explicit Scripture quotation in Art. I; metaphysics of necessary vs contingent being. The necessary-being doctrine recalls Exodus 3:14 (I AM WHO I AM), but Baron cites no Scripture here, so there is no Bible link.

title: Only God is being by essence: existence is of the divine essence, not of the creature
english: Article II. The second division of real being is proposed, and it is proved that God alone is being by essence.

This division is into being by essence and being by participation. Being by essence is the glorious God, who exists by the force of his own essence. Beings by participation are created beings, which have no actual and real existence in the world except as communicated and participated from another by whom they were produced — that is, from God. But that it may be understood how God is said to exist by the force of his essence, let these foundations be held.

First: the existence of God is of his essence. That is, it is not something superadded to the divine essence, nor ought it to be conceived by us as something superadded to it, but it is something included in the very essence of God, no less than animality or rationality is enclosed in human essence. This is shown thus: every substantial perfection is of the essence of God (for the essence of God would not be of infinite perfection if some perfection were granted which his essence does not enclose in itself); but existence is a substantial perfection, as is plain to anyone; therefore it is of the essence of God. Just as, therefore, it is of the essence of a human being to be an animal, or a body, or a substance, so it is of the essence of God to be something actually existing.

2. On the contrary, it is neither necessary nor possible that the existence of a creature be of its essence. It is not necessary, because the essence of a creature is not of infinite perfection. It is not possible, because whatever is of the essence of a thing necessarily belongs to that thing, and its affirmation of that thing is necessary and of eternal truth. But existence does not stand thus in creatures: for I do not truly say, it is necessary that a rose exist, or it is necessary that thunder exist — for they can fail to exist. Yet I do truly say, it is necessary that a rose be a flower, or that thunder be a sound, even when rose and thunder do not exist. Hence it is plain that these latter are essential predications, but not those former. This reason proves not only that existence is not of the essence of a creature, but also that existence does not necessarily follow the essence of a creature or flow from it. For whatever is essential by flowing forth is necessarily affirmed of the thing to which it is essential; but actual existence (as has been said) belongs to creatures contingently. Meanwhile we admit that the capacity or potency for existence belongs not contingently but necessarily and essentially to every real being, whether created or uncreated; but the same is not to be said of actual existence.

3. Let the second foundation be this. If anyone asks whence it is that God exists and cannot fail to exist, no reason can be given except this one: namely, because his essence is of infinite perfection — that is, it encloses every perfection in itself, and therefore existence also. Hence it is plain that God is rightly said to exist by the force of his essence. But if the question is moved concerning creatures — whence it is that they now actually exist — one must not answer that this happens because such is their essence, or because that is the condition of their essence; for their essence is indifferent to existing and not existing — that is, it can exist or not exist at the will of God. Rather one must answer that the true reason of that fact is that their essence, which earlier was only possible and apt for existing, has now been given the very act of existence by God and by secondary causes. Creatures therefore cannot be said to exist by the force of their essence, but by the force of the causes from which they were produced, and chiefly of the first cause. Hence it follows that they are not beings by their own essence, but by participation and reception of existence from the first cause. Besides, the reason of this matter can be given from this very clear foundation: it is the condition of the divine essence that it cannot fail to exist, and that it cannot participate its existence from another; but it is the condition of a created essence that it can, at the will of the first cause, have existence or not have it, and that it cannot exist except by participating the act of existence from the first cause. Hence it is plain that the first cause exists by the force of its essence; but secondary causes, or created beings, do not exist by the force of their essence, but through the action of the first cause from which they receive actual existence.

4. Third foundation. The essence of a creature is rightly and truly called potency; but the existence of a creature may well be called an act superadded to the essence. This is declared thus: just as physical matter is called potency and physical form act, because matter in itself and from itself has no form, but is capable of form, or can receive form, so the essence of a creature can be called potency, because it neither encloses existence in itself nor has it from itself, but is capable of it, or can receive it and participate it from the first cause. But on the contrary the essence of God stands far otherwise: for in itself it encloses the act of existing; and therefore it does not stand toward existence as potency toward act — for no potency encloses act in itself, but is referred to act as to something external. And so much concerning the division of being into finite and infinite.
translator_notes: Exercitatio Prima Art. II from the 1658 Oxford corrected reprint.
No explicit Scripture in Art. II; three foundations on essence and existence. Tip exemption: 0 warranted Bible links OK.

title: God alone is pure act: real being divides into actual, potential, and mixed
english: Article III. The third division of real being is set out, and it is explained how God is pure act.

1. Third, real being is divided into that which is merely actual, that which is merely potential, and that which is partly actual, partly potential — or mixed from potency and act. Merely potential being is that which does not exist in act, but can exist: such a being is a rose in winter. It is to be noted here that philosophers commonly say that those beings which do not exist in act, but can really exist, are in objective potency. For the object of the productive potency which is in causes is that which is producible by the causes — or that which has not yet received existence from the causes, but can receive it. Therefore some possible being, so long as it does not exist in act, is the object of the productive potency of causes, and for that reason is said to be in objective potency, because namely it has that potency which belongs to things so long as they are objects of some causative potency. But when that being has been produced in act and has received existence from causes, it is no longer the object of the productive potency of causes, and on that account is said not to be in objective potency.

2. Merely actual being, or pure act, is the glorious God, to whom this supreme and perfect actuality is ascribed: first, to mark his simplicity. For every composition from potency and act is repugnant to him — that is, from some potential or imperfect principle, and an actual principle; that is, one that actuates and perfects that other principle, as we shall later declare in the doctrine concerning God. Second, to remove and exclude every potency that argues some imperfection. Now there are three kinds of potencies which, on account of their imperfection, cannot be ascribed to God: namely objective potency, which is nothing other than the producibility of a thing by its causes; second, passive potency, which belongs to things insofar as they can suffer and be changed by some agent; third, potency toward non-being. The first potency belongs to things that do not exist, and therefore cannot be ascribed to God, who exists necessarily and never could fail to exist; the two latter belong to things that do exist, yet are mutable and passible: but God is immutable and impassible. But of active potency the account is far otherwise. For active potency, as the metaphysicians have well observed, rather deserves the name of virtue or faculty than of potency: for each thing acts insofar as it is in act, whence the very power of acting is a certain actuality. But someone will ask: every potency is more imperfect than its act; and whatever is imperfect, whether absolutely or comparatively, is to be removed from God. It is answered that even active potency in creatures is often more imperfect than its act, and that because the perfection of a creature is placed in the operation and exercise of the potency, and it is more perfect when it acts than when it does not act: but God does not stand thus. For his supreme and infinite perfection, or beatitude, is placed in this — that he is God — and therefore he does not stand better or more perfectly when he acts than when he does not act.

3. Being that consists of potency and act is finite being actually existing in the world. And a being of this sort is said to consist of act and potency, or to be partly actual, partly potential, for two reasons. First, because in finite beings various compositions are found: namely from genus and difference, from matter and form, from integral parts, from essence and existence; from existing essence and subsistence superadded to it, from subject and accident. Now in all these compositions (that alone excepted which is from integrating parts) there is one potential and receptive principle, which on that account is called potency, and another actual and perfective principle, which on that account is called act: the principle of the former kind underlies in every composition, and the principle of the latter kind is superadded to it. Hence it is plain that finite beings are rightly said to be composed of potency and act. The second reason is this: finite beings, although they exist in act and thus have some act and perfection, are nevertheless not merely actual and perfect, but have those three kinds of potencies that argue imperfection. For first, before they exist, they have that objective potency toward existing. Second, when they exist, they have passive potency, and a receptive potency for new accidents. Third, they have potency toward non-being: for they can be abolished by the first cause and reduced to nothing.
translator_notes: Exercitatio Prima Art. III from the 1658 Oxford corrected reprint (tip to FULL densify past Art. I-II).

title: Fourth division of real being: modes of existing — per se versus in another
english: Article IV. The fourth division of real being is set out, which is drawn from the modes of existing.

1. A fourth division of real being can be drawn from the modes of existing — that is, from modes superadded to the act of existence. For in every being that exists in act these three things can be considered: first, that it has such an essence and nature by which it is constituted in a definite genus of being and is distinguished from all other beings; second, that it exists in act in the world, and so has an act of existing superadded to its essence; third, that it has such a mode of existing as suits its nature. For singular and complete substances are and exist in such a way that they are not in another, but exist through themselves. Singular accidents, by contrast — this whiteness, this blackness — are and exist in such a way that they do not exist through themselves, but in another. Hence it is clear that there are two general modes of existing, superadded to existence itself: the former is the perseity of existing, or the mode of existing through itself and not in another; the latter is the mode of existing in another and not through itself.

2. These things being laid down, the fourth division of real being can be conceived thus: every real being either exists in such a way that it can in no way inhere in another or be communicated to another; or it exists in such a way that it is in act in another, or at least can be in another. For example, this man, this horse, this stone in no way inhere in another by way of a part, or of an essential form, or of an accidental form, or of a quasi-form. By contrast their members inhere in them by way of parts, and their accidents inhere in them by way of accidental forms. I said "or at least can be in another" on account of human souls separated from the body, which, although they are not in act in another, can nevertheless be in another after the manner of parts. But that these things may be better understood, the kinds of those things which can in some way be said to be in another by way of a part or of a form must be enumerated.

3. First, accidents exist in their subject; second, parts both essential and integral exist in their whole; third, the total and singular nature of a thing is in that whose nature it is, after the manner of a form. For the nature or essence of a thing stands as a form; that of which it is the essence stands as matter. Therefore not only does a universal nature inhere in singulars, but a singular nature also inheres in that suppositum whose nature it is. Thus the singular nature of Peter is in Peter himself — that is, it is included in Peter. For Peter is not the humanity of Peter, but something consisting of his singular humanity and of the subsistence superadded to it; and therefore his singular humanity is said to inhere in him.

4. Whatever can be referred to these three classes must be said not to subsist, or to exist through itself, but to inexist in another (if one may so speak). Those things, however, which are referred to none of those classes are said to subsist, or to exist through themselves. For subsistence is nothing other than a certain mode of existing by which some being exists in such a way that it in no way inheres in another thing, but is underlaid and supposed to the other things that inexist in it. Hence a being of this kind is called in Latin a suppositum, in Greek a hypostasis.

5. It is to be noted here that these words hypostasis and subsistence are highly ambiguous and have six significations, of which the first three are less proper and not customary among philosophers, while the last three are more philosophical. First, hypostasis or subsistence is taken for the subsisting thing itself — that is, for a suppositum or person. Second, for true being, not for an empty appearance of it, and likewise for fixed and permanent being. Third, for that which underlies in any way: after which fashion in a building the foundation, in a column the base, in wine the dregs, in urine the sediment, are called hypostasis and subsistence.

6. But among philosophers, to subsist is taken first for being through itself — that is, not in a subject of inherence. In this way every substance, and substance alone — whether universal or particular, whether complete and total or incomplete and partial — is truly called a subsisting being, or a being through itself, not existing in another; accidents, by contrast, do not in this way subsist, but exist in another. Second, that is said to subsist which does not exist in another in such a way that it depends on it as to the act of existing — that is, so that because of its imperfect mode of existing it cannot exist outside that other and through itself. In this signification we deny that not only accidents but also universal substances subsist, and that because they depend on the first things as to actual existence; for they exist in them and by their benefit. Second, we deny that matter, and all substantial forms educible from the potency of matter, subsist in this way: for they so depend on the suppositum in which they inhere that they cannot exist through themselves and outside every suppositum. I said "forms educible from the potency of matter" to exclude the human soul, whose case is otherwise, as will presently appear. I said "outside every suppositum" because matter can indeed exist outside this or that particular suppositum — as outside Socrates or outside Plato — for when they are dead it can enter the constitution of another suppositum and be sustained by it; yet it cannot exist outside every suppositum. Third, we deny that singular substances themselves, when signified by abstract names — that is, the singular essences of created substances — subsist in this way. For the singular humanity of Peter so exists in Peter himself that it cannot exist through itself and outside every suppositum; likewise the singular humanity of CHRIST so exists in CHRIST that in an ineffable manner it depends in its being on his most glorious person. Although therefore singular men exist through themselves and in no way in another, singular human natures nevertheless do not exist through themselves, but in their singular supposita — that is, in men. Someone will say: a singular man and a singular human nature are the same. It is answered that that is most false; for a singular man is not a singular humanity, but something consisting of a singular human nature and of the subsistence superadded to it, as will appear in what follows. Hence the second person of the Trinity is said by the theologians to have assumed a singular human nature, not a singular man.

7. But on the contrary, in this signification we attribute subsistence, first, to all singular complete and predicamental substances — that is, those signified by a concrete name — such as this man, this horse; and likewise to the persons of the adorable Trinity, and that because all these exist in no thing as parts, or as essential or accidental forms. Second, in this sense we also assert that the Divine essence or Deity, although it exists in the three persons of the adorable Trinity, truly subsists; and we say the same of the human soul, although it is in the body as form in matter, and in the composite as a part in the whole — and that because neither does the essence of GOD depend in its being on the divine persons (for that would argue imperfection), nor does the rational soul depend on matter and the composite; for it can exist without them, and it really does exist when it is separated from the body.

8. Third, that is said to subsist which exists in another neither in act nor in potency — that is, which cannot be included in any suppositum. In this signification subsistence is denied to all those things which exist in some suppositum, whether or not they depend on it as to the act of existing. In this way we deny that the human soul and the most glorious essence of GOD subsist: for the former is in man as a part in the whole; the latter, in an ineffable manner, exists in the three persons of the Trinity. And therefore in this sense we say that only, and all,..supposita subsist and have subsistence: for every suppositum so exists that it can in no way exist in another suppositum, as an accident in a subject, a part in a whole, or a nature in that which has the nature. Hence it is that the philosophers say a suppositum is something incommunicable to many, and altogether unfit for existing in another. From these things it is clear that in this fourth division of being, subsistence is to be taken in this last way: for in it, by a subsisting being I understand that which in no way inheres in another, as an accident in a subject, a part in a whole, or a nature — whether universal or singular — in its suppositum. But by a being inexisting in another I understand that which is in some way communicable to another — that is, apt to inhere in another.
translator_notes: Perseitas existendi: Baron's term for the mode of existing through itself (per se), not in another.
Suppositum / hypostasis: the concrete complete singular that underlays inhering natures and accidents.

title: Explanation of being, essence, existence, subsistence, suppositum, and person
english: Article V. An explanation of these words: Being, Essence, Existence, Subsistence, Suppositum, and Person.

1. Essence is accustomed to be described by the philosophers in various ways. First, thus: the essence of a thing is that which is explained by the definition. Second, thus: essence is that through which a thing is constituted in a definite genus of being and is distinguished from all others. Third, thus: essence is the first, radical, and intimate principle of all the actions and properties of a thing. For example, the principles of many human operations are habits existing in the souls of men; the principles of the habits are natural potencies flowing from the essence; the principle of the potencies is human nature or essence; but human essence itself, consisting of soul and body, has no productive and effective principle of itself existing in the man — that is, nothing can be found in the man himself from which his essence flows or is caused. I said that it has no effective principle existing in the man, because it is certain that it has constitutive principles, both physical and metaphysical. Since therefore the natural potencies of things, and the operations of the potencies, draw their origin from the essence, while the essence has no efficient cause prior to itself in that thing whose essence it is, it is rightly called the first, radical, and intimate principle of all the properties and actions of the thing.

2. Finally, essence can not inconveniently be described thus: essence is that which belongs to a thing most necessarily and first of all. I say "most necessarily" to exclude common accidents, which are contingently present to that thing whose accidents they are. I say "first of all" to exclude proper accidents, which, although they belong necessarily to their subject, do not yet inhere in it first; rather the essence inheres first, from which they flow. This, then, is the general rule: whatever inheres in a thing most necessarily, first of all, and intimately, that is the essence of the thing; but whatever inheres either contingently, or on account of another from which it flows — and likewise whatever is adventitious and not intimate — that is something superadded to the essence, not the essence itself.

3. Existence differs from essence chiefly in office and function. For the office of essence is to constitute a thing in a definite genus of being and to distinguish it from all others. Thus a man through his essence, inasmuch as he is a rational animal, is distinguished from all other beings. But the office of existence is to bring it about that a thing having such an essence is outside its causes (as the metaphysicians speak), or rather, that it is outside the virtue and productive potency of causes. For when a thing does not exist, it is said to be in the potency of its causes, because it is producible by its causes and can exist through their effective potency; but when it has been produced in act and has received the act of existing, it is no longer in the effective potency of the causes, but has been led out from the state of potentiality into the state of actuality. While that state lasts, it is not producible through the potency of the causes; for it must perish, and lose the act of existing which it already has, before it can again be produced by its causes and receive existence.

4. This office of existence differs from the office of essence in that the office of essence in all things is stable and perpetual; whereas the office of existence in some things is subject to various changes, because existence itself is now present, now absent. For example, the existence of a rose, or of thunder, at certain times exercises its office, but at other times does not — as in winter, when the rose or thunder are in the potency of their causes, as they say. By contrast, the essence of these and similar things perpetually exercises its office: for whether a rose exists or not, a rose is a flower, by nature and essentially distinct from all other flowers; and the physicists have science of the rose even when it does not exist, because they know the rose to be a flower distinct from other flowers not only by nature or essence but also by properties, virtue, and efficacy. For it is not to be thought that when a rose does not exist it loses its essential distinction from other flowers, or is confused with them as to essence. From these things this definition of existence can be gathered: Existence is a mode superadded to essence, bringing it about that a thing having that essence is outside its causes in the world.

5. These words — essence and existence — having been explained, it is easy to know what Being is. For Being differs from essence and existence as a concrete from two abstracts; and likewise as that which has, from those things which are had from it. For Being is nothing other than that which has essence, or existence. It is to be noted here that Being is taken in two ways, participially and nominally, as they speak. Being, as it is the participle of the verb "to be," signifies that which is existing in act; but Being, inasmuch as it is a verbal noun, signifies that which has an essence capable of existence, whether it exists in act or not; and as Suarez speaks, it signifies being itself, not as exercised in act, but in potency or aptitude. Thus "living," as it is a participle, signifies the actual use of life; but as it is a noun, it signifies only that which has that essence which can be a principle of vital operation.

6. Subsistence properly, and taken in the third signification, agrees with existence in this, that neither this nor that is Being itself, or the essence of Being, but a mode of Being. Yet it differs from it, first, in that existence extends more widely than subsistence: for the former belongs to all things, both substances and accidents; the latter belongs only to singular complete substances, inasmuch as they are signified by concrete names — to this man, this horse, this lion. For as I warned in the previous article, this singular humanity or this singular horseness do not subsist, but exist in their supposita and by their benefit.

7. From these things that have already been said we can gather that, in any singular substance signified by a concrete name, these three acts can be discerned: first, the act of the singular essence, through which that substance is such an individual, distinct from all others; second, the act of existence, through which the substance that has such a singular essence is outside its causes in the world; third, the act of subsistence, through which it is so outside its causes that it does not inexist, or lean upon another, but underlies those that inexist in it, and is supposed under them — whence, as was said above, it is called a suppositum.

8. The suppositum is easily known once the nature of subsistence is known; for a suppositum is nothing other than that which has subsistence, thus superadded to essence and existence — or that which, in the act of existing, leans upon no other, but is laid under and supposed by other things that lean upon it. It can also be explained thus: a suppositum is that which is in no way communicable to many, and likewise in no way can inhere in another, after the manner of a part or of a form. Therefore Peter's singular humanity is not a suppositum, because it is truly said to be in Peter; likewise the human nature of Christ is not a suppositum, for the same reason; but Peter himself is a suppositum, because he does not inhere in another as a part in a whole, an accident in a subject, or a nature in that which has a nature. In the same way Christ, and any other person of the Trinity, is a suppositum for the same reason. Accidents are not supposita, whether they are universal or singular, because they inhere in and lean upon their subjects. Universal substances also are not supposita, because they are communicated to singulars and inhere in them. Finally the glorious God, insofar as he is common, in an ineffable way, to the three persons of the Trinity, is not a suppositum — and that because it belongs to the account of a suppositum that it cannot be communicated, or inhere in another suppositum; but God, or the Godhead, is communicated and inheres in the three persons of the Trinity.

9. Person differs from suppositum in this, that every person is a suppositum, but not every suppositum is a person: for a person is nothing other than a suppositum endowed with reason — whence it is described by Boethius thus: It is an individual substance of a rational nature. Therefore suppositum in general is divided into rational and irrational. A rational suppositum is called a person; an irrational suppositum, as this horse, this stone, does not have a peculiar name imposed upon it. Person is divided into created and uncreated. The uncreated persons are three: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. A created person is either angelic, as Gabriel, Michael; or human, as Peter, John.
translator_notes: Suarez is named in the Latin for the participial vs nominal distinction of Ens.
Art. V §§7–9 close: three acts in the concrete singular; definition of suppositum; person vs suppositum (Boethius). Densify fill 2026-09-21.

title: Whether in creatures the suppositum and its singular nature really differ
english: Article VI. Whether, in creatures, the suppositum and its singular nature really differ.

1. I have not resolved here to air that celebrated controversy concerning the distinction and diversity of essence from existence — whether namely it is real, or of reason alone. For that question has no usefulness in theology, and is more thorny and more difficult than can be grasped by those who are raw and beginners in metaphysics. Yet concerning the distinction of subsistence and of nature or essence I will say a few things: for the determination of that question has a notable use in theology.

2. This question is accustomed to be proposed in two ways. First, thus: whether, in created supposita, subsistence is something positive and really distinct from the singular essence to which it is superadded — or whether it is not. Second, thus: whether the suppositum and its singular nature really differ — for example, whether Peter and his singular human nature are in truth the same, or whether Peter, as Peter, includes something real and really diverse from his singular nature. Whether the question is proposed in this way or in that, it is the same controversy; and therefore I briefly answer that Peter and his singular nature really differ, as the including and the included, or as the composite and its constitutive principle. For every created suppositum, as Peter, includes the singular nature and something superadded to it — namely subsistence; or (to speak more plainly) every created suppositum is really composed of the singular essence and the subsistence superadded to it, which some call suppositality, others personality. If therefore we compare the suppositum to the singular nature, they are distinguished as whole and part; but if we institute the comparison between the singular nature itself and subsistence — as between Peter's singular human nature and Peter's subsistence or personality — then they are contradistinguished from each other as two extremes composing that created suppositum, namely Peter. But that this sentence may be established, first it must be proved that subsistence, or suppositality, is not a mere negation, as Scotus opines, but is something positive constituting Peter together with the singular nature, insofar as he is a suppositum. Second, that that positive thing differs not by reason alone but really from the singular nature with which it constitutes Peter. From this I will then manifestly infer that Peter really differs from his singular human nature, and that his human nature is truly and properly said to be in him. For if Peter, insofar as he is Peter, or insofar as he is a certain particular human person, includes these two — namely his singular humanity and his personality — as two constitutive principles really distinct, it is necessary that his singular humanity really differ from him, and be in him as truly as either his matter or his form is said to be in him.

3. Scotus, in book 3 of the Sentences, distinction 1, question 1, says that every suppositum, besides the singular nature, also includes subsistence, but he asserts that subsistence is a mere negation of the aptitude or potency of being in another suppositum. For singular natures have a potency of existing in a suppositum; but the suppositum itself, as Peter, cannot be in any other suppositum; and therefore on his view the suppositum, as such, is constituted by the negation of this potency of existing in a suppositum. This sentence is rightly rejected by Francisco Suárez, Metaphysical Disputations 34, section 2. First, because the subsistence which the suppositum adds to the singular nature is a certain substantial perfection; but a mere negation cannot be a substantial perfection; therefore a mere negation is not subsistence. Second, if subsistence, or personality, were a mere negation, the three persons of the Trinity would be constituted in their personal being, and would be distinguished from one another, by negation alone — for they are distinguished by their subsistences or personalities; but this is absurd, and plainly destroys the mystery of the Trinity. Therefore subsistence is not a mere negation, but something positive superadded to the singular essence for constituting the suppositum.

4. It must now be proved against Durandus, in book 1 of the Sentences, distinction 34, that subsistence is something really diverse from the essence or singular nature of created substances (for concerning God one must think far otherwise). And that is clearly shown by this reason: the Word assumed a singular human nature, but did not assume a human suppositum or human person — for thus he would not be one simple person, but twin. Therefore the human suppositum and its singular nature are really diverse; and therefore something is in truth included in the human suppositum besides its singular nature; and this can be nothing other than subsistence, or personality.

5. This reason is also accustomed to be proposed thus: those things which can be really separated are not really the same; but subsistence can be separated from the singular nature; therefore they are not really the same. The assumption is proved: the Word assumed a singular human nature; but he did not assume human personality or human subsistence, as all theologians confess; therefore they can be separated. This reason not only proves that subsistence really differs from the specific nature, which is common to all individuals, but also from the individual or singular nature; and therefore that their sentence is openly false who say that Peter's subsistence or personality is his individual difference. For Christ did not assume human nature in common, but a singular humanity; and he did not assume a singular person. In truth, therefore, the singular person differs from the singular nature, and includes something that is not included in the singular nature — namely subsistence and personality.

6. By these two reasons it is clearly proved that every suppositum, besides its singular nature, includes something positive really distinct from that nature — namely subsistence; and on that account that every created suppositum is really composed of its singular nature and subsistence, which others call suppositality. Someone will say: if subsistence is something real, really distinct from essence, it is either matter, or form, or the composite itself, or some accident of it. I answer: that which in the constitution of the suppositum is superadded to the singular nature is not some being properly so called, but a mode of being; and therefore it is neither matter, nor form, nor the composite, nor an accident of it.
translator_notes: Scotus In Sent. 3 d.1 q.1 and Suárez Disp. Met. 34 sect. 2 are named in the Latin; Durandus In Sent. 1 d.34 likewise. Logos = the Word.

title: Why philosophers attribute composition from essence and existence, and from essence and subsistence, to created substances but not to God
english: Article VII. What is the cause why philosophers attribute composition from essence and existence, and likewise from essence and subsistence, to created substances, but not to God.

1. Created singular substances can be considered in three ways, as was said above. First, insofar as they have such an essence. Second, insofar as they are beings actually existing in the world. Third, insofar as they have such a mode of existing, or insofar as they are supposita. If they are considered in the first way, they have composition from the physical parts of their essence, and from the metaphysical parts of the same: for example, if Socrates is considered insofar as he is a man, he is physically constituted from his matter and form; likewise metaphysically, or logically, from genus and difference — that is, from animal and rational. If singular substances are considered in the second way, they include two things, namely essence and existence, which according to our way of conceiving stand as potency and act, as I explained above: and therefore, since from potency and act there is always made some composite that is one through itself, we rightly say that singular substances so considered are composed from essence and existence — that is, from nature and the act of existing. Thus Peter, insofar as he is a man actually existing in the world, includes these two: human nature, and the act of existing; he includes them (I say) as two principles from which he is constituted.

2. If created singular substances are considered in the third way — that is, if they are considered insofar as they are supposita, not only having an essence actually existing in the world, but also such a mode of existing, namely through itself and not in another — if (I say) they are so considered, they include two things, namely an essence actually existing, and subsistence, or the mode of existing through itself, superadded to that existing essence: but the essence or singular nature of a created substance is potency with respect to subsistence, and subsistence is its act superadded to it and perfecting it; and therefore from an essence or nature actually existing, and from subsistence superadded to it, we rightly say that something one through itself comes to be — namely the suppositum itself. Thus Peter, insofar as he is such a person, includes a singular essence, through which he is a singular being, and a singular subsistence, through which he is a singular person.

3. Someone will ask what the cause is why these three compositions are not attributed to God: since essence, existence, and subsistence or personality are found in all the persons of the Trinity, no less than in human and angelic persons — for each person of the Trinity has its essence and existence, common to it with the remaining persons of the Trinity; it also has its own proper subsistence, or personality, through which it differs from the remaining persons. The answer is that none of their composition can be attributed to God, his simplicity being preserved, and likewise the infinite perfection and dignity of that most glorious nature. But this will become plain if we consider and weigh those compositions one by one and apart.

4. First, then, essential composition, both physical and metaphysical, is to be removed from God: the former indeed, because it overturns a spiritual nature; the latter, because God is contained under no univocal genus, as will afterwards be proved (God favoring) in the questions concerning God. Second, composition from essence and existence is removed from God for two reasons: first, because for every composition, whether it be real or of reason, it is required that one thing be superadded to another for the constitution of some third; but existence is neither in truth, nor according to our way of conceiving, something superadded to the essence of God, but rather is something included in God's essence itself, as I declared in Article II. Therefore the existence of God cannot concur with his essence to constitute some third thing. Second, composition from essence and existence is attributed to created substances because their being so stands as potency, and existence as an act superadded to it; but the essence of God cannot be called potency with respect to the divine existence, because it includes existence in itself, as was said in the place already cited: and no potency includes its act in itself, but is directed to its act as to something further and external.

5. Concerning the third composition, which is that of supposita from singular nature and subsistence, there is greater hesitation: for it seems that it ought to be attributed to God, because each person of the Trinity includes these two: the divine essence, which is common to all three persons; and its particular personality, through which it is distinguished from the remaining two persons; therefore it is composed from these two. If you reply that some person is not composed from nature and subsistence because subsistence is something included in God's essence itself, just as was already said of existence, you will easily be refuted: for if the subsistence or personality of the Father were of his essence, it would be common to the whole Trinity, just as his essence itself also is. But this is absurd: therefore that too. Concerning this controversy I will set out my mind in several assertions.

6. Assertion 1. The subsistence, or personality, of the Father (let the same be said of the hypostasis of the Son and of the Holy Spirit) does not differ from his essence by any kind of real diversity, neither as a thing from a thing, nor as a mode of a thing from a thing, but differs from it by a distinction of reason alone. This assertion is proved thus: first, whatever is in God is God. Therefore nothing is in God that in truth, and on the side of the thing (as they say), differs from his Godhead. Second, if the person of the Father is really composed from his essence and subsistence or personality, two absurdities will follow: First, that God the Father is not, absolutely speaking and in the highest degree, simple; for the highest simplicity takes away every composition, and above all a real one: second, that the Godhead is a part of some thing; but every part is something incomplete, and less perfect than that whole of which it is a part.

7. Assertion 2. God is not composed from nature and subsistence by such a composition as is seen in created substances. This assertion plainly follows and is inferred from the preceding: for if God is not really composed from nature and subsistence, he does not have such a composition from nature and subsistence as created substances have; for these are composed from nature and subsistence as from two principles distinct in the thing itself, and therefore their composition is real.

8. Assertion 3. Although the subsistence of the Father is not of his essence, but according to our way of conceiving is something superadded to his essence, it is nevertheless not lawful to say that the Father's person is composed from those two by a composition of reason; indeed we ought not to conceive those two in the Father as two parts composing him: for when we conceive the Godhead as a part of some thing, we form an enormous concept of God, and we invent for God an imperfection that is not small. Wherefore the modesty of those seems praiseworthy and to be imitated, who piously think and profess that essence and personality are included in the person of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, not by way of composition, but by way of an ineffable conjunction or union.

title: Given that every perfection is of God's essence, does personal subsistence follow; and is God, as communicable to three, a person (Cajetan)
english: Article VIII. This being laid down — that every perfection is of the essence of God — whether it follows that personal subsistence is of his essence; and whether God, insofar as he is communicable to the three persons of the Trinity, is a person, as Cajetan maintains.

1. From the preceding doctrine there arises a difficulty of no small weight concerning subsistence or personality: for since it has been established that every perfection is of the essence of God, it seems necessarily to follow that subsistence, or personality, is included in his essence; and therefore that God, insofar as he is common to the three persons of the Trinity, is a suppositum or person. The reason of the connection is this: because subsistence is a certain substantial perfection, and that not a slight one; for every suppositum has a more perfect mode of existing than the nature which exists in the suppositum. Here, therefore, two things are to be discussed: first, whether personal subsistence is of the essence of God; second, whether God, as God, is a certain person common to the whole Trinity.

2. That the former difficulty may be removed, after two observations have been set down beforehand, I will propose my sentence in several assertions. First it is to be held that subsistence is taken by the philosophers in three ways, as was said above: for (1) those things are said to subsist which do not exist in a subject of inherence; (2) those which do not so inexist that they depend, as to the act of existing, upon those in which they inexist; (3) those which in no way inexist in another suppositum, or can inexist in one. Second it is to be held that to these three significations of this word a fourth can be added, which, although it is less frequent, is nevertheless no less proper. For that being can be said to subsist which so exists that it depends in its being upon no creating or conserving cause: this mode of existing is proper to God, and cannot be communicated to any created being; and therefore it is without doubt the most perfect mode of existing.

3. These things being laid down, let this be Assertion 1. Subsistence taken in the first and second way is essential to God, and equally common to the Trinity: for just as it belongs essentially to God to exist in act, so also it is of the essence of God so to exist that he neither exists in any subject, nor depends, as to the act of existing, upon that suppositum in which he is.

4. Second Assertion. Subsistence taken in the third way, although insofar as it is in God it does not differ in the thing from his essence, nevertheless cannot truly be said to be of the essence of God: for whatever is of the essence of God belongs to God as God. If therefore personality is of the essence of God, God insofar as he is God is a person, and consequently all three persons, insofar as they are one true God, can truly be called one person: which is plainly absurd, and contrary to the principles of our faith.

5. Assertion 3. Subsistence taken in the fourth way is of the essence of God, or is an essential attribute of his: for to be the first Being, having its being from itself and not from elsewhere, is the very nature or essence of God.

6. Assertion 4. This word "perfection" is to be distinguished; for some are perfections whose negation imports imperfection — as to be or to exist, to live, to be a Spirit, to be good, to be just: for their opposites, namely not to exist, not to live, and so on, are manifestly imperfections. Others are perfections whose negation imports no imperfection: thus the most wise decrees of God concerning the creation and governance of things are perfections, but their negation imports no imperfection: for even if God had had no such decrees, indeed even if he had had decrees contrary to these, he would not have been more imperfect. So to walk, to run, to sit, to speak are perfections of a human being — for they are acts, and every act is a perfection: but the negation of those acts involves no imperfection; although the negation of the potencies from which they arise brands the thing to which it is attributed with a mark of imperfection. I say that the negation of these acts involves no imperfection, because a human being is not more imperfect when he does not walk than when he walks, or when he does not speak than when he speaks.

7. All perfections of the former kind are of the essence of God, and necessarily belong to him as God: but concerning perfections of the second order one must think otherwise; for they are not of the essence of God, nor do they necessarily belong to him as God — for example, the decrees of God concerning the eternal salvation and death of human beings, although they do not differ in the thing from his essence, are nevertheless not truly said to be of the essence of God: for if that were true, they would be in God by the necessity of nature, and thus the liberty of the divine decrees would be taken away. To this latter genus of perfections we refer personal subsistence; for although its negation, when it is attributed to the finite essence of creatures, involves imperfection, yet when it is attributed to the Godhead, or to the divine nature, it imports no blot of imperfection. The reason of the disparity is this: the divine essence includes in itself a certain mode of existing far more perfect than personal subsistence — namely the mode of existing without dependence in being upon any creating or conserving cause. I say that this mode of existing is more perfect than personal subsistence, because in it is placed the perfection of the first being; and on that account it cannot be communicated to creatures: but personal subsistence is communicated both to human beings and to angels. On the contrary, the finite essence of creatures includes in itself neither the act of existing, nor any mode of existing more perfect than personality: and therefore it is imperfect on account of the defect of personality, whereas the Godhead is in no way imperfect on account of the lack of such subsistence.

8. Francisco Suárez, On the Trinity book 3, chapter 10, brings forward another distinction of perfection; but a more obscure and difficult one, and therefore I will not propose it here. But this is carefully to be noted which he adds to that distinction — namely, that divinity, the personal relations or subsistences being prescinded, does not formally include their perfections; yet it includes them eminently, both because this is necessary for the infinity of that being, and because the Godhead itself is the root and foundation of all those perfections.

9. The latter question is easily solved once the former difficulty has been removed: for since that subsistence which is proper to supposita does not belong to God as he is common to the three persons, it is to be said without fear that God so considered is not a person. But (says Cajetan) God, insofar as he is common to the three persons, although he is not a person strictly and properly speaking, can nevertheless be called a complete person. I answer with Fonseca that in divine things novel and unused locutions, abhorrent from every custom of the Fathers, are not to be employed — especially since someone can be deceived by such a manner of speaking and suppose that the three persons are one person, or one suppositum.

title: Whether God, as common to the three persons, is a singular substance; and whether the three persons of the Trinity are three singular substances
english: Article IX. Whether God, insofar as he is common to the three persons, is a singular substance; and whether the three persons of the Trinity are three singular substances.

1. Among the Latins, substance is so called from subsisting (as some will have it) and from standing under accidents (as others will have it). According to the latter etymology, God Most High is not a substance, but the principle and cause of all substances; but according to the former, he is most truly and most properly a substance — not indeed a universal substance, but a singular and individual one. For second substances stand in need of first substances, that they may exist in them; but God, even insofar as he is common to the three persons, stands in need of no thing in which to exist. But someone will object: God, insofar as he is common to the three persons of the Trinity, is predicable of several; therefore he is a universal, and a second substance. I answer that the definition of the universal is to be conceived thus: a universal is that which can be predicated of those things that are several according to the very name of the universal. Thus man is predicated of those that are several according to the name of man — that is, of several men. But God is indeed predicated of several persons; yet he cannot be said to be predicated of several according to the name of God — that is, of several gods. Others say that that is universal which can be predicated of several, in which it is divided and multiplied: but it comes to the same thing.

2. Second objection: no first or singular substance contains under itself other first or singular substances; but God contains under himself three persons; and each person is a singular substance. Reply: no singular substance contains under itself other singular substances numerically — that is, distinct by individual differences; yet one singular substance can contain under itself several persons that have one essence numerically, and are distinct only by modes of existing.

3. The other question proposed in the title is this: whether the three persons of the Trinity are three singular substances. The difficulty of this question is set here: that the orthodox Fathers hold the Son to be ὁμοούσιον with the Father — that is, as the Latin Church translates it, consubstantial, or of one and the same substance; so that Jerome rightly said in his Letter to Damasus, Who would dare with a sacrilegious mouth to grant three substances in God? On the contrary, since a person is a singular substance, there seem to be as many singular substances in the Godhead as there are persons in it.

4. The determination of this question can be comprised in two assertions. First: new and unused locutions are not to be employed in the mysteries of the faith; for all manners of speaking that seem to favor heretics, even in appearance, are to be avoided. Those therefore who speak of the three persons of the adorable Trinity ought not to use the aforesaid manner of speaking, saying that they are three substances — lest they seem to favor the Arians, the Macedonians, Valentinus Gentilis, and his followers. Second: that locution can in no way be admitted, but is to be rejected as openly false and tritheistic. For if the three persons are three substances, they are either three finite substances, or three infinite substances. They are not three finite or created substances, as is plain; nor yet are they three infinite substances, because there are not three gods.

5. The consequence is not valid of the argument brought on the other side. For I will give a like consequence which is plainly vicious and inept in the judgment of all: as if someone should argue in this way — Peter standing, Peter sitting, and every other aggregate of that sort, is a singular substance clothed with a certain accident; therefore as many as there are such aggregates, so many are there singular substances clothed with accidents. If (I say) someone should argue thus, the inference will be vicious: because Peter standing and Peter sitting are two such aggregates; yet they are not two singular substances, but one substance numerically and individually. Someone will ask what can rightly and legitimately be gathered from this antecedent — a person is a singular substance. It is answered that this is a just and lawful consequence: a person is a singular substance; therefore as many as there are persons, so many are there those things to each of which it belongs to be a singular substance.

title: Whether Christ, as man, is a person; and whether Christ, as man, is everywhere
english: Article X. Whether Christ, insofar as he is man, is a person; and whether Christ, insofar as he is man, is everywhere.

1. These arguments seem to prove the affirmative part of the question. 1. Just as all singular oxen, horses, lions, and so on, are irrational supposita, so also all singular human beings are rational supposita, or persons: therefore Christ, insofar as he is a singular man, is a person. 2. Every complete singular substance, signified by a concrete name, is a suppositum, as all the metaphysicians teach; but Christ, insofar as he is a singular man, is such: therefore he is a suppositum; and every rational suppositum is a person. 3. A singular human being differs from his singular essence as a suppositum differs from the nature existing in the suppositum; therefore Christ, insofar as he is a singular man, is a suppositum, and consequently a person.

2. Next, if Christ, insofar as he is man, is a person, as has now been proved, he is either an immense person existing everywhere, or a finite person comprehended in a definite place. The latter cannot be admitted, because then there would be two persons in Christ, one finite and the other infinite; therefore the former must be said — namely, that Christ, insofar as he is man, is an immense person, existing in every place and beyond every place. And therefore it must be confessed not only that the proposition 'Christ the man is everywhere' is true, but also that 'Christ, insofar as he is man, is everywhere' is true.

3. That this question may be satisfied, I say first that the proposition 'Christ, insofar as he is this man, is a person' is ambiguous, and therefore to be distinguished. For as Suárez speaks on the third part of St Thomas, volume 1, question 16, article 11, that particle 'insofar as' either reduplicates the suppositum or reduplicates the nature — that is, either this is its sense: Christ, by reason of the human nature assumed by him, is a person; and so the proposition is openly false, for Christ neither has from his humanity that he is a person simply, nor has he from it any new subsistence or personality; for then there would be a double hypostasis in him; nor is it true to say that the humanity assumed by him has its own proper subsistence or personality, because it inexistes in another and does not subsist. Therefore it is to be denied that Christ is a person by reason of his human nature. Or this is its sense: Christ, insofar as he is a suppositum including human nature, is a person; and so the proposition is most true, as those three arguments placed at the threshold of the article prove; for that suppositum in which the humanity is, is a person.

4. Others answer more briefly that Christ, insofar as he is this man, includes two things — namely, the divine subsistence and the human nature — and they say that Christ, insofar as he is man, is a person with respect to the divine subsistence, which he includes materially, but not with respect to the assumed human nature, which that word 'this man' more formally and directly imports.

5. I say second that that manner of speaking — 'Christ, insofar as he is man, is a person' — is to be fled. 1. Because it seems to favor the Nestorian dogma by which two persons are attributed to Christ. 2. Because reduplication properly taken imports the proper reason or cause why the attribute is in the subject; but it is certain that the reason according to which personality belongs to Christ is not in the human nature, and therefore Christ is not sufficiently conveniently called a person insofar as he is this man. 3. Because when theologians discuss Christ and use those reduplications 'insofar as God', 'insofar as man', or 'insofar as this man', they do not look to Christ's personal subsistence, but to the nature: for they designate the nature according to which these or those attributes belong to Christ. But personality does not belong to Christ according to the human nature, and therefore that locution is unusual: 'Christ, insofar as he is this man, is a person'.

6. As for the other part of the argument, the answer is as above: Christ, insofar as he is this man, includes two things — namely, the divine subsistence and the human nature superadded to it. With respect to the divine subsistence, which he includes in a certain material way, it can be said that Christ, insofar as he is this man, is an immense person and defined by no place. With respect to the human nature, which that word 'this man' more formally and directly imports, it is rightly denied that Christ, insofar as he is this man, is an immense person existing everywhere; and that because his human nature has its particular ubi and is comprehended in a definite place.

7. For the rest, although that proposition is true in some sense, as has now been said, yet because it smells of the Ubiquitarians' error, and because the sense which the words of that proposition more evidently carry before them is absurd — namely, that Christ by reason of the human nature is immense, or that his humanity is immense — therefore it is to be rejected and carefully avoided.

title: Whether the Ubiquitarians' arguments drawn from the personal union are valid
english: Article XI. Whether the Ubiquitarians' arguments drawn from the personal union are valid.

1. The first objection of those who invent a certain immensity of Christ's human nature is customarily put thus: Whatever is personally joined to the whole Logos exists wherever the Logos exists; but Christ's human nature is such: therefore. The answer is that the proposition is openly false; for from the personal union of the two natures in Christ it no more follows that the humanity is wherever the Deity is, than from the substantial union of our soul with the matter of the head it follows that the matter of the head is wherever the soul is — that is, that it is in the foot, because the soul is in the foot: I say that it is substantially joined to the whole soul, because the whole soul is in the whole body, and whole in each of its parts. If therefore the Ubiquists argue well and acutely when they construct such a syllogism, this argumentation will be good and effective: What is substantially joined to the whole soul exists wherever the soul exists; but the matter of the head is substantially joined to the whole soul: therefore it is wherever the soul is; but the soul is in the matter of the foot; therefore the matter of the head also is in the matter of the foot.

2. Second objection. The union of the two natures in Christ was made indivisibly and without interval: therefore one of them does not exist except where the other exists — that is, they coexist in all places. Answer: the adverbs 'inseparably' and 'indistantly', when used to explain the manner in which those natures are united in the person of the Logos, have a twofold use. First they are used to refute Nestorius's error, who not only distinguished these natures but divided and separated them, assigning to each nature its own proper hypostasis, and therefore did not join them into one hypostasis. Second, that we may know that that union is indissoluble, and that these natures, once they have been joined, can never be disjoined or separated. We therefore deny that consequence: the human and divine natures are indissolubly and inseparably joined in one person; therefore wherever one of them exists, there the other also exists. The reason is that by the distinction of the local presence of the two natures their union is not dissolved, but rather the truth of the natures is asserted and confusion is removed.

3. Someone will press first: If one of those natures exists there where the other does not exist, then one of them is separated from the other; but the former is true: therefore the latter also. Answer by denying the connection: for the human soul, which is whole in the matter of the head, is also whole in the other members in which the matter of the head does not exist; yet the union of the soul with the matter of the head is not by this means dissolved: for, as all know, the soul is torn away and separated from the head and the remaining members only by the death of the human being. Second instance: The soul, which exists whole in the matter of the head and whole outside it, is not united to the head by an adequate and complete union, but is united to it as to a partial and incomplete matter; whereas by an adequate and complete union it is united to the whole body, because the soul is so whole in the whole body that in no way is it outside it. Therefore, since on the Calvinists' view the whole Deity exists in the humanity and also whole outside it, the union of the Logos with the humanity will not be adequate and complete. Answer: the reason is unequal. For the union of the soul with the matter of the head is called incomplete because it is not a union of whole with whole — that is, of the whole form with the whole matter, but with a part of it; but the union of the Logos with the human nature is of whole with whole — that is, of the whole Deity of Christ with his whole humanity, in one hypostasis. The true reason, therefore, why the union of the soul with the matter of the head is inadequate is not that the soul exists outside the matter of the head, but that it is not a union of whole with whole — that is, of the integral form with the integral matter. Wherefore it is not that the Ubiquitarians should object against us that we dissolve the person of Christ, tear apart his natures, and invent an inadequate conjunction of natures for him; on the contrary, we grieve and marvel that such feeble arguments, such childish absurdities, could please and impose upon men distinguished for learning.

4. Third objection. The second person of the Trinity, after he assumed human nature, is always and everywhere GOD INCARNATE: therefore he is nowhere UN-INCARNATE, as Philip Nicolai insolently speaks. Answer: that argument concludes nothing against us, and therefore the whole of it can be admitted. For since the incarnation of God, once posited, consists in the assumption of human nature and its hypostatic conjunction with the divine, it is necessary that 'excarnation' (to speak with Philip Nicolai) signify the depositing, deserting, and dissolving of the union already made: but far be it from us to say that the most blessed Logos anywhere deposits, strips off, or expels from his hypostasis the flesh which he assumed in the Virgin's womb. Someone will press first: if the Logos exists outside the flesh, then he is somewhere un-incarnate; but the former is true on your view; therefore you are bound to admit the latter also. Answer by denying that connection; for just as the whole human soul exists outside the matter of the head with its union to the matter of the head preserved, so also the whole Logos exists both in the flesh and outside the flesh with his personal union to the human nature preserved; and therefore 'to be outside the flesh' does not necessarily infer excarnation, or the dissolution of that personal union. Matthias Martinius, a most acute theologian, answering an argument of this kind proposed by Balthasar Mentzer, says that the little word 'outside' is ambiguous; and that sometimes it is equivalent to 'beyond' — that is, it denies the inclusion of one thing in another; but sometimes it imports separation and denies union. In the former way he says the Logos exists outside the flesh assumed by him, but not in the latter way.

5. Someone will press second: If the Logos, in the former way, is outside the humanity, then somewhere he will not be man; but the Logos is nowhere not man: therefore he is nowhere outside the humanity. The assumption is proved: the Logos is always and everywhere man, for he is always and everywhere the God-man. Answer: Although Saint Thomas, and with him nearly all the scholastic theologians, think that proposition 'the Logos is everywhere man' simply false, yet I judge that a distinction is to be applied. For either this is its sense: the Logos everywhere is a person having human nature united to himself; or this is its sense: the Logos is a person having human nature united to himself everywhere, and therefore locally present to himself everywhere. In the former sense the proposition is true and is admitted by us, because it does not contradict our position; but in the latter it is plainly false, and therefore is never admitted by us. That there is a huge difference between these two senses of that proposition is clear from these examples: 'A husband everywhere, or wherever he exists, is a man having a wife' is a true proposition; but this, 'a husband is everywhere, or in all places, having a wife', is a false proposition. Likewise this, 'A master everywhere is a man having a servant', is a true proposition; but this, 'A master is a man, everywhere having a servant'.

6. Someone will press third: If the Logos does not have human nature united to himself everywhere and locally coexisting, then whole Christ is not everywhere, but only one of his natures, namely the Deity; but the latter is absurd: therefore the former also. Answer by denying the connection of the proposition; for from the antecedent of that connected proposition it follows well that the whole of Christ — that is, all the parts of Christ — is not everywhere; but it does not follow well that whole Christ is not everywhere. Why Doctor Jacob Andreae, and with him the remaining Ubiquitarians, should repudiate this distinction, I greatly wonder. For whole Christ is man, but not the whole of Christ; whole Christ suffered, died, and rose again; but not the whole of Christ — that is, both of his natures.

7. Someone will press fourth: Christ is not whole without the humanity: therefore if whole Christ is everywhere, the humanity of Christ is everywhere. Answer by denying the sequel; for the consequence of that argument is plainly ridiculous and unworthy of refutation, as is clear from these examples which contain a like consequence: Whole Christ is not without the Deity: therefore if whole Christ suffered and died, the Deity also suffered and died. Likewise, Christ is not whole without his foot: therefore if whole Christ is a man, the foot of Christ is a man.
